en: A Warning to the World:

Failing to embody the fundamental Way, beings are submerged in birth and death—among those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation, whether moving horizontally or vertically, flying or sinking.
Among these, those who lose their human form are like the soil of the great earth, while those who obtain a human body are like the dust upon a fingernail.
Among human beings, they are mostly born in frontier regions or among the lowly and base; even if born in the Central Kingdom, they may receive a female body.

If they are men, they are crippled, deformed, or afflicted by a hundred maladies. Even if they should obtain the ten marks of a full-grown man, they dwell in a world of fear during the time of the five turbidities.
With a body of flesh and a life of breath, within a single lifetime they are like sparks from a stone or a wind-blown lamp.
The setting sun and its lingering rays last but a moment. Among them, those who do not meet with untimely death are beyond counting.
Even those who attain the full span of human life, reaching the age of sixty, are but one in ten thousand.

Should one happen to reach the age of maturity, excluding the period of childhood ignorance, from thirty to forty is already considered wealthy; let us take approximately thirty years for that interval. Within this time...
Illness, calamity, sorrow, and distress occupy more than half of one's existence. Thus, as the ancients said:
"In the brief month of this floating life, there are only four or five days during which one can truly laugh with open mouth. Therefore, we know that anxiety is long-lasting while joy is fleeting;
pleasure is scarce while suffering is abundant. It is as if standing upon a perilous peak ten thousand fathoms high, or dwelling within a vast ocean of a thousand fathoms deep. Even if...
Having attained a modicum of pleasure, one must still contemplate drifting and sinking. Now, birth exerts me through dwelling in the womb; old age robs me of my youthful vigor;
illness impairs my physical appearance; death destroys my spiritual essence. Honor indulges me in arrogance and luxury;
disgrace shatters my spirit; nobility makes me haughty; meanness frustrates my conduct; wealth allows me to be unrestrained.
I am greedy. There is poverty that afflicts my livelihood; there is pleasure that agitates my emotions; there is suffering that pains my spirit.
There is praise that gives rise to arrogance in me; there is disparagement that destroys my reputation. Even when cold, it oppresses my body;
when heat, it vexes my breast; when thirsty, it dries my throat; when hungry, it weakens my belly; when startled, it terrifies me.
My vital essence (*po*) is lost through fear; my soul (*hun*) is disturbed by anxiety; my will is ruined by vexation. Compliance nourishes my attachment;
opposition gives rise to my aversion. Intimacy entangles my emotions; estrangement engenders my resentment. Harm brings about the destruction of my body; sorrow knots my intestines.
Thus, encountering objects gives birth to the mind, and following circumstances moves the thoughts—whether toward what is beautiful or...

Neither of these evils accords with my heart’s intent; both prolong the cycle of karma and utterly destroy the root of the Way. Some may even further deceive their sovereign and rebel against their fathers;
they treat all things with arrogance and rush after the times. Their hearts are like beasts and their intentions like foxes; they seek only profit and pursue fame at any cost.
They deceive people and flatter their conduct; they align themselves with power to exploit the solitary. They deepen their calamities and exalt their karmic deeds.

They fan the fire and blow upon the wind; they raise the dust and turn their backs on awakening. They propagate heterodoxy and estrange themselves from the truth. They look only to their past errors while neglecting what lies ahead;
they plot with their mouths to depart, never considering the return. Seeking only life, they know nothing of extinction; thus, moment by moment, they are scorched and boiled as they walk.

I walk along the moats and ditches. If one should now obtain even a single *kṣaṇa* in this world, one must accumulate benevolence and compassion, practice goodness to cultivate the mind, and eliminate evil.
As the Book says: "When one performs good, a hundred auspicious signs descend upon them; when one performs what is not good, a hundred calamities descend upon them.

Therefore, all the various causes and conditions of the world—whether adverse or favorable—and the empty suffering of body and mind that we undergo in vain, are all due to our ignorance of the Three [Treasures].

The realms are but a single mind. This is because the first five consciousnesses—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—as well as the eighth consciousness, all obtain their objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

there are no phenomena external to the mind. It is by means of the sixth, the clearly discerning mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), that external objects are constructed through inferential reasoning (*anumāna*).
These are entirely produced by conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and arise following recollection (*anusmṛti*). If there were no conceptualization, the myriad phenomena would have no form. Therefore...
The Sūtra says: "When ideation ceases, there is stillness; when consciousness halts, there is non-action. It further says: "All phenomena are not solid; they exist only in dependence upon thought.

One who skillfully understands and perceives emptiness has no conceptualizations whatsoever. If one realizes the essential principle of the One Mind, then naturally, outside of the mind, there is no phenomenon that can be described.
How could there be any concern for joy or sorrow, or any interference with the thoughts of right and wrong? As a Buddha-verse says: "Not yet..."
One realizes that objects are merely mind and gives rise to various forms of discrimination. Once one has realized that objects are merely mind, discrimination no longer arises.
Having understood that objects are merely mind, one then abandons the appearances of external dust; from this point, discrimination ceases, and one awakens to the equality of true emptiness.
Therefore, the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states: "All objective realms are merely the deluded movement of the mind. If the mind does not arise, all objective realms [cease]."
Characteristics are extinguished; there is only the single true mind pervading all places. Therefore, the three realms are false and illusory, produced solely by the mind.
Apart from the mind, the objects of the six sense-fields do not exist, nor do any conceptual discriminations. Such discrimination is itself one's own mind. The mind does not see the mind;
no characteristics can be apprehended. As the former masters said: "To hold that there are dharmas external to the mind is to revolve within the cycle of birth and death. External to the mind...

There is no other way; birth and death must be forever abandoned. As a sutra says: "All phenomena that arise are manifested solely by the mind. A treatise states: "In the three realms there are no separate dharmas; they are all created by the one mind.
Once one has faith in this one mind, one must unite with it through meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). As a sutra says:
"If one were to teach the sentient beings of a trichiliocosm to practice the ten wholesome deeds, it would not equal the merit of a single meal [of dharma]."
Recently, while in a state of single-minded stillness, I entered the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic.

If one can clearly and profoundly realize one's own mind, then through the union of this concentration and wisdom, one will be able to remain unmoved by worldly afflictions and shall immediately achieve perfect enlightenment. Nothing encountered throughout one’s life can surpass this.
May future worthies be universally moved by this; it is fit to be inscribed upon their sashes.
